questions.title: What sets the two limits?
opts: Its upper limit by an abiotic variable such as drying out; its lower limit by biotic interactions such as competition.
Its upper limit by biotic interactions such as competition; its lower limit by an abiotic variable such as drying out.
Both of its limits by abiotic variables such as drying out, because biotic interactions do not change along the shore.
Both of its limits by biotic interactions such as grazing, because abiotic variables are the same all along the shore.

questions.title: Barnacles X and Y: which niche?
opts: Competition with Y keeps X on the upper shore: the middle shore is in its fundamental niche, not its realized niche.
Drying out keeps X on the upper shore: the middle shore is outside its range of tolerance and its fundamental niche.
Y preys on X on the middle shore: the middle shore is in its realized niche, but not in its fundamental niche.
X and Y share one realized niche: X moves down only because the middle shore becomes drier when Y is removed.

questions.title: Sea lettuce missing at both ends
opts: Top: drying out at low tide is outside its range of tolerance. Bottom: brown seaweed outcompetes it for space.
Top: brown seaweed outcompetes it for space. Bottom: drying out at low tide is outside its range of tolerance.
Both ends: limpets graze it faster than it grows, because limpets are found all along the transect.
Both ends: the rock temperature is outside its range of tolerance: too hot at the top, too cold at the bottom.

questions.title: A range of tolerance at 34 °C
opts: Its upper limit is set by an abiotic variable: it can live only where the rock stays at or below about 30 °C.
Its upper limit is set by grazing: with no limpets it could grow on the upper shore, even at 34 °C at low tide.
Its realized niche reaches higher than its fundamental niche, because there is less competition on the upper shore.
Its upper limit is set by its competitors: with them removed, it could survive the 34 °C of the upper shore.

questions.title: How to sample periwinkles
opts: Count them in each quadrat, as for limpets, and search the cracks inside the quadrat as well.
Estimate their percentage cover, as for barnacles, because they are too small to count one by one.
Use capture–mark–release–recapture, because every animal that lives on the shore is motile.
Leave them out, because a quadrat can be used only for sessile organisms such as the seaweeds.

questions.title: Biased quadrat placement
opts: The mean is too high, because bare rock is never sampled: the positions are chosen, so they are biased.
The mean is less precise but still unbiased, because every quadrat is still divided into 100 small squares of cover.
The mean cannot be calculated, because percentage cover needs quadrats placed side by side along a belt.
The mean is unchanged, because the same quadrat size and the same way of counting are used every time.

questions.title: Transect time and quadrats
opts: 33 minutes; 40 quadrats
30 minutes; 40 quadrats
33 minutes; 20 quadrats
30 minutes; 20 quadrats

questions.title: Cover or count for limpets
opts: Limpets are separate individuals, and density is a number of individuals per unit area, so they are counted.
Limpets move about during the low tide, so their cover changes while it is estimated, but a count does not.
Percentage cover is used only for plants and seaweeds, never for animals such as limpets or barnacles.
Percentage cover can be estimated only along a continuous belt transect, never in quadrats placed at random.

questions.title: Lincoln index: an estimate too high
opts: Some crabs lose their marks before the second sample, so fewer marked crabs are caught again.
Marked crabs are easier to catch than unmarked crabs, so more marked crabs are caught again.
The second sample is larger than the first, so more crabs in total are caught on the second day.
No crabs are born or die between the two samples, so the size of the population stays the same.

questions.title: Cover with the seaweed not lifted
opts: B’s estimates are too low wherever seaweed grows, so B’s data show barnacles falling too steeply towards the sea.
B’s estimates are better, because only the barnacles that can be seen from above count towards the percentage cover.
B’s estimates are as valid as A’s, because the two students simply make different random errors in their counting.
B’s estimates are too high, because seaweed that lies on the rock looks like barnacles when it is seen from above.

questions.title: Random squares that cluster
opts: Keep them: random positions can fall close together by chance, and moving them by choice would bring back bias.
Move the next quadrats lower in the area, so that the 30 quadrats are spread evenly over all of the 5 m × 5 m area.
Start again with new numbers, because a random sample is not valid unless its quadrats are spread out evenly.
Add five quadrats on the green patches by choice, so that both species have a fair chance of being recorded.

questions.title: Degrees of freedom of a 3 × 2 table
B. State a correlation, with its evidence
D. Conclude from a chi-squared test
E. A limitation and an improvement
F. Link the data to niches
Your turn 1: Describe a relationship: brown seaweed and rock temperature
Your turn 2: Evaluate a statement about sea lettuce
Clumped or spread at random?
opts: They are clumped: many quadrats hold none and a few hold several, so the counts vary more than chance gives.
They are spread evenly: most quadrats hold about one limpet, so the counts vary less than chance gives.
They are spread at random: each limpet settles by chance alone, so the counts vary about as much as chance gives.

questions.title: All the limpets in the area
Chi-squared: expected values
opts: With expected values below 5, one quadrat more or less changes χ² a lot, so the test is unreliable.
With expected values below 5, χ² can never pass the critical value of 3.84, so the result is never significant.
With expected values below 5, there are no degrees of freedom, so no critical value can be read from the table.

questions.title: A bigger quadrat
opts: More quadrats will hold both species, so a negative association becomes harder to detect.
Fewer quadrats will hold both species, so the negative association will look stronger than it is.
Nothing will change, because presence and absence do not depend on the size of the quadrat.

questions.title: When to measure the temperature
opts: The rock heats up during the low tide, so the time of each reading changes it, not only the place on the shore.
Temperature probes read too low on wet rock, so the readings near the water’s edge are wrong, not the timing.
There is no problem, because an abiotic variable such as the rock temperature stays the same all through a low tide.

questions.title: The Lincoln index: its assumptions
opts: No crabs enter or leave the area between the first sample and the second sample.
The marks stay on the crabs overnight and can still be seen clearly in the second sample.
Marked crabs mix fully with the unmarked crabs in the area before the second sample is taken.

questions.title: Temperatures read 90 minutes apart
opts: Part of the 9 °C difference may come from 90 more minutes of sun, not from the position on the shore.
Holding the probe on the rock for 30 seconds is too short a time to give a reading of its temperature.
The upper shore is normally cooler than the lower shore, so a 9 °C difference must be an error in reading.
Readings taken at different times can never be used in one correlation, so all the data must be deleted.

questions.title: Two people, two estimates
opts: One person estimates the cover in every quadrat, so any error is the same in all of them.
Each person estimates half of the quadrats, so the work is shared and finished sooner.
Always record the higher of the two estimates, so that no organism is left out of the data.
Stop estimating cover and record only presence or absence, because cover is never reliable.
